concepts.name: LangGraph time travel: replay and fork

choices.text: Only `escalate`, since a returned `Command` replaces the static edge
Both `escalate` and `log`, since the static edge still runs as well
Only `log`, since a static edge takes priority over any `goto` value
Only `escalate`, and the `level` update is dropped without a reducer

questions.explanation: `Command` only adds a dynamic edge. The static edge from `add_edge` still runs, so both `escalate` and `log` follow `triage`. That is why the docs say to use either `Command` or static edges for a node, not both. The `update` is applied as usual; a reducer only decides how updates to the same key combine.

sources.title: Graph API overview (LangGraph, Python)
sources.claim: Return `Command` from a node to update state (`update`) and route (`goto`) in one step; use conditional edges when you only route. `Command` only adds dynamic edges: static edges defined with `add_edge` still execute, so use either Command or static edges for a node, not both.

questions.prompt: You move your agent's background workers to Fargate Spot to save money. What notice does a running task get before AWS takes the capacity back?

choices.text: A two-minute warning, sent as SIGTERM and as an EventBridge event
None: the task is stopped at once, like a crash, then started again
Fifteen minutes, enough for the agent run in progress to complete
A two-minute warning, then Fargate moves the task to on-demand

questions.explanation: Before a Spot interruption, the task gets a two-minute warning, as a SIGTERM to the task and a task state change event in EventBridge. Fargate does not fall back to on-demand capacity: a service retries on Spot until capacity is available. So Spot suits work that can stop and resume, not runs that must finish.

sources.title: Amazon ECS clusters for Fargate
sources.claim: Fargate Spot runs interruption-tolerant tasks at a discount; before a Spot interruption a two-minute warning is sent as an EventBridge task state change event and a SIGTERM to the task. Fargate doesn't replace Spot capacity with on-demand; containers must handle SIGTERM or get SIGKILL after `stopTimeout` (default 30 s, up to 120 s).

questions.prompt: An agent run on a LangGraph thread went wrong at step 4 of 7. How would you replay it from an earlier checkpoint, and fork it with a corrected state? Say what gets re-executed.

model_answer.summary: Find the checkpoint with `get_state_history` and invoke from its config to replay, or call `update_state` on it to fork; either way, only the nodes after that checkpoint run again.
key_points: Use `get_state_history` to find the checkpoint, then invoke the graph with that checkpoint's config to replay from it
Nodes before the checkpoint aren't re-executed; nodes after it run again, including LLM calls, API requests and interrupts, so results may differ
`update_state` doesn't roll the thread back: it creates a new checkpoint branching from that point, and the original history stays
The update goes through the node's writers, reducers included (`as_node` picks the node), and execution resumes from that node's successors

questions.explanation: Time travel is how you debug and explore agent runs: replay to reproduce, fork to try a fix. The common mistake is thinking a replay is free or identical: everything after the checkpoint runs again for real, which costs tokens and can call tools twice.

sources.title: Use time travel
sources.claim: Use `get_state_history` to find a checkpoint and invoke with its config to replay: nodes before it are not re-executed, nodes after it re-execute, including LLM calls, API requests and interrupts. `update_state` does not roll back a thread: it creates a new checkpoint branching from that point, applies values through the node's writers including reducers, and execution resumes from that node's successors; the original history stays.

questions.prompt: When should a LangGraph node return a `Command` instead of you adding a conditional edge?

choices.text: When the node must update state and pick the next node in one step
Whenever it routes at all, because conditional edges are deprecated
Only when it calls an LLM, since edges can't read the model's output
When it must run a few nodes in a fixed order, without changing state

questions.explanation: `Command` combines a state update and a routing decision in one return value. If a node only needs to route, the docs say to use a conditional edge instead. Conditional edges are not deprecated, they can read any state (model output included), and a fixed order is just static edges.

questions.prompt: Your Fargate Spot workers run long agent jobs. What must the container and task definition do so a Spot interruption doesn't lose work?

model_answer.summary: Treat the two-minute warning as a graceful shutdown: catch SIGTERM, stop or checkpoint the job within `stopTimeout`, and make sure the job can be picked up again, because Fargate won't move it to on-demand.
key_points: The process must handle SIGTERM; if it ignores it, the task gets SIGKILL after `stopTimeout`, which can lose or corrupt data
Set `stopTimeout` in the container definition up to 120 seconds (the default is 30) to get more time to clean up
Use that time to checkpoint or requeue the job so another worker can resume it
Fargate doesn't replace Spot capacity with on-demand, so a service retries on Spot, and a one-task service is down until capacity returns

questions.explanation: Spot is cheap because it can be taken away. A worker built for it treats interruption as normal: save progress on SIGTERM, keep jobs resumable, and don't rely on a single Spot task for anything that must always be available.

questions.prompt: You call `update_state` on a past checkpoint of a LangGraph thread to fix a bad value. What happens to the thread's history?

choices.text: Later checkpoints are deleted, and the thread rolls back to that point
The old checkpoint is edited in place and keeps its checkpoint ID
A new checkpoint branches off from it, and the old history is kept
Nothing changes until you compile the graph again with the fix in it

questions.explanation: `update_state` doesn't roll a thread back. It creates a new checkpoint that branches from the one you chose, and the original execution history stays intact, so you can compare the fork with what really happened.
